# MCP tool reference

This is the exhaustive catalogue generated from the live `raptor-studio` server: **68 tools** (67 with `--no-render`), **8 resources** and **3 prompts**.  For installation, client setup, concepts and task recipes, start with the [MCP guide](MCP.md).

Every tool section is generated from the server's `tools/list` payload.  It repeats the full description the assistant sees, turns the input schema into a typed parameter table, lists the declared return fields, and gives one argument example.  A trailing `?` is not used here: the **Required** column is authoritative.

## How to read a tool section

- **Kind** is the MCP risk hint: `read-only` changes no model, `writes` edits a model or workspace, and `destructive` deletes or reverts.  It is a coarse hint, not the `--read-only` gate: `simulate`, `start_run` and `open_model` carry `writes` because they create run or workspace artefacts, but `--read-only` allows them.  The gate refuses tools that create, edit or delete models or export files; opening, analysis and simulation stay available.
- **Parameters** comes from the tool's input schema.  `Required` means the server rejects the call without it; **Schema default** is the literal default in the schema (`—` when it gives none); `Enum / allowed values` lists every accepted value.  Where the generator knows a tool computes a real default from the model or another setting, that is called out under the table; otherwise the schema value is all the catalogue can claim.
- **Returns** lists the top-level fields of the declared output schema.  `Always present` is yes when the field is in the schema's `required` list.
- **Example** is an argument object, not a whole JSON-RPC envelope.  Put it in your client's tool form or send it as the `arguments` of `tools/call`.  Replace `<model_id>`, `<run_id>`, `<job_id>` and `<model_id_a>`/`<model_id_b>` with ids from another call.

### Workspace and lifecycle

Find bundled examples, open or create a model, and manage its workspace lifetime.

<a id="tool-close_model"></a>

#### `close_model`

- **Kind:** destructive
- **Group:** [Workspace and lifecycle](#tools-workspace)

Close one or more models.  Set delete=true to also remove their files.

`model_id` accepts a single id or a list, for cleaning up several
scratch/sweep models in one call. Each id is closed independently and
only the ids you pass are affected -- other open models are never
touched, whatever their names. One bad id doesn't abort the rest; the
failures are reported alongside the successes.

`delete=true` removes that model's own workspace directory (its
`model.rbds`, backups and meta) and is **irreversible** -- the undo
history goes with it. It does not delete exported files (use
`delete_file`) or runs.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `delete` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `model_id` | string \| array<string> | yes | — | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | array<any> | yes |
| `failed` | object | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>"
}
```

<a id="tool-create_model"></a>

#### `create_model`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Workspace and lifecycle](#tools-workspace)

Create a new model.

template: 'blank' (default), 'series' (n blocks in series),
'parallel' (n in parallel), or 'k_of_n' (k-of-n voting of n blocks).
Non-blank templates are auto-laid-out on the shared layered grid, so
the diagram renders cleanly without a separate `auto_layout` call.
Returns {model_id, summary}.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `k` | integer | no | `1` | — |
| `n` | integer | no | `2` | — |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — |
| `template` | string | no | `blank` | `blank`, `series`, `parallel`, `k_of_n` |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes |
| `summary` | string | yes |

**Example**

```json
  "name": "Pump station",
  "template": "series",
```

<a id="tool-save_model_as"></a>

#### `save_model_as`

- **Kind:** destructive
- **Group:** [Workspace and lifecycle](#tools-workspace)

Save a model to a file path.

The path must be inside the workspace or an --allow-write directory.
format: 'rbds' (default) or 'rbd'.  If `path` has **no extension** the
format's own extension is appended (so `"out"` -> `out.rbds`).  An
explicit extension must match `format`; a mismatch or a path into the
managed models/runs/renders trees is refused.  A .rbd export runs
validate() first and refuses on ERROR. The layout is saved as it is;
`layout_warning` says when an .rbd viewer would draw elements overlapping
(call `auto_layout` first to space them out).

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Returns**

| `layout_warning` | null | yes |
| `path` | string | yes |

### Build and edit

Create a whole model from one spec, edit elements and links, configure behaviour, and step through undo history.

<a id="tool-add_block"></a>

#### `add_block`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Add a block to the model.

`fail_dist`/`repair_dist` take a distribution name ("Weibull") or a
code from `list_distributions`.
Numeric parameters accept expression strings with a `#` comment for
traceability, e.g. "0.00015 * 20000 / 8760  # failure rate".  `after`
wires the new block after an existing element name/id, which must not
already have its one link out. A block takes at most one incoming and
one outgoing link (RAPTOR Studio) -- to feed it from/to more than one other
element, route through a Node (`add_node` + `connect`; see `connect`).
Returns {block_id, name, warnings}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `after` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `fail_dist` | integer \| string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `fail_params` | array<number \| string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — |
| `parent` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `repair_dist` | integer \| string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `repair_params` | array<number \| string> \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `block_id` | string | yes |
| `name` | string | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "name": "Pump",
  "fail_dist": "Exponential",
  "fail_params": [
    1000
  ],
  "repair_dist": "Exponential",
  "repair_params": [
    10
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-add_elements"></a>

#### `add_elements`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Add many blocks, nodes or events with one save.

Each item is `kind` plus the same fields the single add tool takes:

- block: `name`, optional `fail_dist`, `fail_params`, `repair_dist`,
  `repair_params`, `parent`, `after`
- node: `name`, `type` (start/regular/end/in/out), `parent`, `k`
- event: `name`, `prob`, `parent`

Items are created in list order, so a later item may use `after` to wire
itself to an earlier one. Atomic: a refused item restores the model.
Returns {added, elements: [{kind, id, name}]}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `elements` | array<object> | yes | — | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |

Parameter notes:

- `elements` — List of {"kind": "block"|"node"|"event", ...fields}

**Returns**

`{added, elements: [{kind, id, name}]}`.

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "elements": [
    {
      "kind": "block",
      "name": "Valve",
      "fail_dist": "Exponential",
      "fail_params": [
        5000
      ]
    },
    {
      "kind": "event",
      "name": "Power available",
      "prob": 0.999
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-add_hierarchy"></a>

#### `add_hierarchy`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Create an empty hierarchy -- a sub-model boundary -- with its In and
Out markers already wired up correctly.

This is the fiddly part to do by hand: each marker's own `parent` must
be the new hierarchy's id (not the enclosing level) and both markers'
`n` must match their real link counts, or the engine crashes on load
with an unhelpful KeyError. Building one through `build_model` means
declaring `in_id`/`out_id`, the two marker nodes with their `parent`
set to the hierarchy's own id, and their link counts -- three
non-obvious constraints.

The hierarchy starts empty and unwired. Add contents with
`add_block(parent=<hier_id>)` (read the id from
`describe_model(detail='full')`, or from the return value here), then
`connect` the In marker to the first element and the last element to
the Out marker. To build a hierarchy *around* elements you already
have, use `collapse_selection` instead -- it does all the rewiring.

**Hierarchies nest at most 8 deep** (a hierarchy inside seven others is
the deepest allowed): plan the levels before building. A hierarchy
whose `parent` is already 8 deep is refused. The result's `depth` is
the new hierarchy's level (1 = on the home level) and `levels_below`
how many more can still go inside it.

Returns {hier_id, name, in_id, out_id, parent, depth, levels_below}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — |
| `parent` | integer | no | `0` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `depth` | integer | yes |
| `hier_id` | string | yes |
| `in_id` | integer | yes |
| `levels_below` | integer | yes |
| `name` | string | yes |
| `out_id` | integer | yes |
| `parent` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "name": "Cooling loop"
}
```

<a id="tool-add_node"></a>

#### `add_node`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Add a node to the model.

type: 'start', 'regular', 'end', 'in' or 'out'.

k: K-out-of-N threshold.  A node's n comes from its *incoming* links,
so set k only after the voting blocks are wired INTO the node.  `-1`
(the default) is RAPTOR's "K-of-N never set" sentinel and is treated
as 1-of-N -- it does **not** mean "all incoming paths required"; use
`k = n` for an all-required node.  It is stored verbatim as `-1`, so
`get_element` reports `k=-1`; the coercion to 1 happens when the model
runs.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `k` | integer | no | `-1` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `name` | string | no | `` | — |
| `parent` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `type` | string | no | `regular` | `start`, `regular`, `end`, `in`, `out` |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | yes |
| `node_id` | string | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "type": "regular",
  "name": "Join",
  "k": 2
}
```

<a id="tool-build_model"></a>

#### `build_model`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Build a complete model from a friendly .rbds spec document.

Give the spec inline as `spec`, or, for a large one, as `spec_path`: a
JSON file **relative to the workspace** (or an `--allow-read`
directory). Exactly one of the two. To open a finished `.rbds` or
`.rbd` file instead, use `open_model`, which takes the same kind of path.

Hierarchies in a spec nest at most 8 deep; a deeper spec is refused.

`build_model` always creates a NEW model. `model_id` is accepted only
to reject it with a clear message: it used to be ignored silently, so
a caller that passed one believed it was appending to that model.
Use `add_elements`/`add_block` to edit an existing model.

`spec` is a JSON object with `blocks`, `nodes`, `events`, `hierarchies`,
`links`, `system`, `experiment`, `rates`, `spare_pools`, `resources`,
`triggers`, `phases` and `annotations`, using the friendly snake_case
fields from docs/RBDS_FORMAT.md (e.g. a block's `fail_dist`/`fail_params`;
distributions may be given by name or code).  Ids
are assigned where omitted, links are wired, counts synced.  This is
the main tool for creating a whole model in one call. A complete
`.rbds` document goes in as `spec={"rbds_text": "<the file's text>"}`.

`experiment` takes the .rbds run block itself (`trials`,
`termination_type`, `term_condition`, `analyses`, `recording`, ...), so
the run settings no longer need a second `configure_system` call.

RAPTOR Studio's input rules apply as they do to every edit: a spec with a link
RAPTOR Studio will not let you draw (Start linked to two blocks, say -- use
Start -> a Node -> the blocks) or a value its dialogs refuse is rejected
with RAPTOR Studio's own message.

`spare_pools`/`resources`/`triggers`/`phases` are lists of dicts built
with the same row constructors the `configure_*` tools use.  Friendly
fields per entry:
- spare_pools: name, stock, new_spares, arrive_every, eso, emer_time,
  slo, level, quantity, slo_time, rso
- resources: name, num_in, spare_cost, fixed_per_use, per_time_unit,
  phases
- triggers: name, init_used, dist, params, repeats
- phases: name, duration_dist, params, mission
- phase_states (top level, needs `phases`): {element name or "Block:N": one
  state per phase}.  Block/event state `"A: 1.000"` (active at that
  stress/probability), `"C: 1.000"` cut, `"L: 1.000"` linked, events also
  `"F"`/`"P"`; node state `"C"`, `"L"` or an integer k.  Elements not
  listed are unphased.
`phases` here does **not** take per-element `assignments` (that needs a
live model) -- build first, then call `configure_phases`.

`annotations` is a list of drawing overlays (text/rect/ellipse/arrow)
placed after auto-layout, so `adjacent_to`/`from_`/`to` resolve to real
element positions.  Each entry takes the `add_annotation` fields (note
the arrow spelling is `from_`); `add_annotation` adds one afterwards.

IDs: a Block, Node, Event and Hierarchy each have their OWN id space
in the file format -- a Block `id=2` and a Node `id=2` are different,
unrelated elements, and RAPTOR Studio itself allows this (every real
fixture this project has captured bears it out). Auto-assigned ids
(when you omit `id`) are allocated from one shared pool across every
kind, so two auto-assigned elements never collide -- but if you set
`id` explicitly, nothing stops you from choosing one that matches an
existing element of a DIFFERENT kind, and downstream tools/reports
always disambiguate by kind (`"Block:2"`, not bare `2`) for exactly
this reason. When giving a selector or a dependency `dep_num` to any
tool, always pair the id with its kind. And because auto-assigned ids
are pooled in section order, any element you intend to reference by
id (`parent`, a hierarchy's `in_id`/`out_id`, a link endpoint,
`dep_num`) should be given an explicit `id` -- the number it would
otherwise auto-receive is not predictable from declaration order.

`auto_layout` (default True) places every element on the shared
layered grid (Start left -> End right) so the model's diagram renders
cleanly; pass False only when the spec carries its own `xPos`/`yPos`
coordinates you want to keep.

Format: `.rbds` is the native, preferred format; only produce an `.rbd`
when the user explicitly asks (via `save_model_as(format="rbd")`).

Capacity analysis: set `system.capacity_analysis: true` and
`system.flow_generated` (the demand), give links `nom_flow`/`max_flow`,
and mark the boundary node(s) with `full_flow: false` — capacity caps
only bind on links entering a node whose unrestricted flow is off.
Link friendly fields: `nom_flow`, `max_flow`, `cap_pri`, `cold_pri`,
`a_prob`, `auto_time`, `man_time`.

Parallel/converging paths: a node's `n` must equal its real incoming
link count exactly (validation refuses the mismatch -- RAPTOR Studio
crashes on it) and every node, including End, defaults to `n=1`. Two
blocks converging on End directly is therefore an error; either give
End `"n": 2` (plus `"k"` if not all paths are required), or route
through an intermediate node first, e.g. for A and B in parallel:
`nodes: [{"name":"Join","type":"regular","n":2,"k":1}, ...]`,
`links: [{"from":"A","to":"Join"}, {"from":"B","to":"Join"},
{"from":"Join","to":"End"}]` (`create_model(template="parallel")`
builds exactly this shape for a plain A||B case).

Returns {model_id, summary, validation}.  A successful build is **not**
the same as a runnable model: check `validation.runnable` -- the build
can succeed structurally while `issues()` still reports engine-gate
errors (e.g. `k > n`).

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `auto_layout` | boolean | no | `true` | — |
| `model_id` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — |
| `spec` | object \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `spec_path` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `validate_model` | boolean | no | `true` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes |
| `summary` | string | yes |
| `validation` | object | no |

**Example**

```json
{
  "name": "Quickstart",
  "spec": {
    "blocks": [
      {
        "name": "Pump",
        "fail_dist": "Exponential",
        "fail_params": [
          1000
        ],
        "repair_dist": "Exponential",
        "repair_params": [
          10
        ]
      }
    ],
    "nodes": [
      {
        "name": "Start",
        "type": "start"
      },
      {
        "name": "End",
        "type": "end"
      }
    ],
    "links": [
      {
        "from": "Start",
        "to": "Pump"
      },
      {
        "from": "Pump",
        "to": "End"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

<a id="tool-collapse_selection"></a>

#### `collapse_selection`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Move existing blocks/nodes/events into a new hierarchy, rewiring the
boundary.

The API counterpart of the GUI's *Collapse Selection*. `selectors` names
the elements (by name, or `Block:N` / `Node:N` / `Event:N`) that should
become the new hierarchy's contents. Links wholly inside travel down a
level untouched; links that crossed the boundary are rewritten to
address the hierarchy, and each is split so the sub-model's own graph
stays complete (the outside half keeps its id, an inside half is added
off the In/Out marker).

An existing hierarchy (by name or `Hier:N`) can be part of the
selection: it moves in whole, with everything inside it, one level
deeper. Start/End/In/Out nodes are refused -- a hierarchy cannot
contain the model's own terminators.

This is the one-call way to wrap a branch you have already built, and
the way to reproduce the book's "three ovals" figures. Read
`describe_model(detail='full')` afterwards to see the new level.

**Hierarchies nest at most 8 deep**: collapsing on a level that is
already 8 deep is refused. The result's `depth` and `levels_below`
say where the new hierarchy sits and how many more fit inside it.

Returns {hier_id, name, in_id, out_id, parent, moved, depth,
levels_below}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `name` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `parent` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `selectors` | array<string> | yes | — | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `depth` | integer | yes |
| `hier_id` | string | yes |
| `in_id` | integer | yes |
| `levels_below` | integer | yes |
| `moved` | array<any> | yes |
| `name` | string | yes |
| `out_id` | integer | yes |
| `parent` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "selectors": [
    "Pump",
    "Valve"
  ],
  "name": "Cooling loop"
}
```

<a id="tool-configure_block_defaults"></a>

#### `configure_block_defaults`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Set the distributions `add_block` uses when you don't name any.

This is the MCP equivalent of the GUI's *Block Defaults* button: set
your house values once and every block you place picks them up, instead
of restating four numbers on every `add_block` call.

- `action='list'` — show the current defaults (`{}` means "use each
  model's own template-row defaults").
- `action='set'` — store the fields you supply; omitted fields are
  left as they are.  `fail_dist`/`repair_dist` are distribution codes
  from `list_distributions`.
- `action='clear'` — forget them and fall back to model defaults.

Precedence at placement time: the arguments you pass to `add_block`,
then these defaults, then the model's own block template row, then the
`rbdlib` canonical values.  Defaults are per-workspace and persist
across server restarts.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | string | no | `list` | `list`, `set`, `clear` |
| `fail_dist` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `fail_params` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `repair_dist` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `repair_params` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `block_defaults` | object | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "action": "set",
  "fail_dist": 4,
  "fail_params": [
    1000
  ],
  "repair_dist": 4,
  "repair_params": [
    10
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-configure_maintenance"></a>

#### `configure_maintenance`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Configure preventive maintenance for a block.

pm_freq: maintenance interval (hours).  pm_duration_dist/pm_params:
the PM duration distribution.  trigger_name: a trigger element (for
triggered PM).

defer_flags: bool-valued PM Options, matching the block Properties
dialog exactly (unknown keys raise an error):
- `spare`: needs a spare on hand to conduct PM.
- `refresh`: after PM completes, refresh the block like new.
- `mis_defer`: defer PM until a non-mission phase occurs (only
  meaningful when the model has phases).
- `req_defer`: defer PM until a spare or resources are available.
- `fail_reset`: a failure resets the time to next PM activity.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `defer_flags` | object<string, boolean> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `pm_duration_dist` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `pm_freq` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `pm_params` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `selector` | string | yes | — | — |
| `trigger_name` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `applied` | boolean | yes |
| `element` | object | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "selector": "Pump",
  "pm_freq": 720,
  "pm_duration_dist": 4,
  "pm_params": [
    4
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-configure_phases"></a>

#### `configure_phases`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Configure mission phases.

phases: [{name, duration_dist, params, mission}].

`mode='replace'` (default) makes `phases` the whole list;
`mode='add'` appends them to the phases already there (cells for the
new phase are filled with Raptor's default); `mode='remove'` deletes
the phases named in `remove` and shifts the rest down.

`unassign` names blocks/events/nodes whose phasing is cleared (flag
off, per-phase cells dropped) -- previously there was no MCP route
for this.

assignments: {element: [per-phase state]}, one list entry per phase
(a short list is an error, not padded).  A block/event state is
`"<code>: <value>"` -- code `A` (Active), `C` (Cut) or `L` (Linked),
value the stress multiplier, e.g. `"A: 1.000"`, `"C: 0.500"`; the
colon and value are required even for Cut (a bare word like "Cut"
crashes the engine's phase parser instead of erroring here). A node
state is a bare token: `"C"`, `"L"`, or an integer k-of-n threshold
for that phase.  Phase rows are always built through rbdlib.make_phase_row.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `assignments` | object<string, array<any>> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `mode` | string | no | `replace` | `replace`, `add`, `remove` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `phases` | array<object> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `remove` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `unassign` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assigned` | integer | yes |
| `phases` | integer | yes |
| `removed` | integer | yes |
| `unassigned` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "phases": [
    {
      "name": "Cruise",
      "duration_dist": "Fixed",
      "params": [
        10
      ]
    }
  ],
  "mode": "add"
}
```

<a id="tool-configure_sparing"></a>

#### `configure_sparing`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Configure sparing for a block.

mode: 'infinite' (default), 'custom', or 'pool'. `spare_pool` is
required for mode='pool' and must name an existing pool (create one
with `manage_spare_pools`).
stock: initial spare count; restock_every: restock interval (hours);
emergency: emergency shipping time (hours); slo: stock level order.
With mode='pool' the POOL's stock and restock interval govern; the
block's own `stock` only applies to mode='custom'.
Returns {applied, warnings}.

| `level` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `mode` | string | no | `infinite` | `infinite`, `custom`, `pool` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `quantity` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `restock_every` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `selector` | string | yes | — | — |
| `slo` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `slo_time` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `spare_pool` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `stock` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `applied` | boolean | yes |
| `element` | object | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json

  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "selector": "Pump",
  "mode": "pool",
  "spare_pool": "Pumps"
}
```

<a id="tool-connect"></a>

#### `connect`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Connect two elements with a link.

`from_element`/`to_element` are either ["Block", id] / ["Node", id]
or a bare element name like "PumpA".

`replace=True` removes any link already leaving the source and any
link already entering the target first, so a wrong connection is
corrected in one call. Without it, RAPTOR Studio's own limit (one link
in/out per element) refuses the second connection.

RAPTOR Studio's link rules apply, and a link it will not let you draw is
refused with its own message, leaving the model unchanged: a block,
event or hierarchy takes at most one link in and one out; a Start or In
marker one link out and none in; an End or Out marker one link in and
none out. Fan-in/fan-out (two blocks feeding one element, or Start
feeding two) goes through a Node: `add_node` first, then connect each
element to it.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `from_element` | any | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `replace` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `to_element` | any | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `link_id` | string | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "from_element": "Start",
  "to_element": "Pump"
}
```

<a id="tool-connect_many"></a>

#### `connect_many`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Create many links with one save.

Endpoints are the same as `connect` (a name, or ["Block", id] /
["Node", id] / ["Hier", id]). Applied as one atomic batch; the model is
written once. Returns {connected, links: [{link_id, from, to}]}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `links` | array<object> | yes | — | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |

Parameter notes:

- `links` — List of {"from": endpoint, "to": endpoint} objects

**Returns**

`{connected, links: [{link_id, from, to}]}`.

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "links": [
    {
      "from": "Pump",
      "to": "Valve"
    },
    {
      "from": "Valve",
      "to": "End"
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-diff_models"></a>

#### `diff_models`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Say what is different between two models (their inputs, not their results).

This compares *the models themselves*: elements added, removed, renamed or
changed (distributions, sparing, maintenance, costs...), connections added
or removed, hierarchy moves, k-of-n changes, system settings, rates, spare
pools, resources, triggers and phases. It runs nothing. `compare_models`
is the other one: it runs models and compares their *results*.

`model_a` / `model_b` are workspace model ids (the reference and the one
changed); open files with `open_model` first, this tool does not load
paths. Elements are paired by name, then by id (`match`: "auto"; "name" or
"id" to use only one; "id" is right for a model against an earlier copy of
itself).

`ignore` lists categories to leave out. The default (omit it) is
["layout", "derived"]: screen positions and columns the file reader
computes. Pass [] to show everything. Categories: layout, derived,
identity, failure, repair, streams, sparing, maintenance, logistics,
dependency, cost, phasing, capacity, structure, system, project, other.

detail="summary" returns the counts, the added/removed/renamed lists and
at most 50 field changes (`truncated` says whether more exist;
`total_changes` counts them); detail="full" returns every change. Each
change has `field`, `label`, `category` and the values `a` and `b`
(distributions are described in words, with raw columns in `a_raw` /
`b_raw`).

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `detail` | string | no | `summary` | `summary`, `full` |
| `ignore` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `match` | string | no | `auto` | `auto`, `name`, `id` |
| `model_a` | string | yes | — | — |
| `model_b` | string | yes | — | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a` | object | yes |
| `b` | object | yes |
| `elements` | object | yes |
| `identical` | boolean | yes |
| `ignored` | array<any> | yes |
| `links` | object | yes |
| `phases` | object | yes |
| `project` | array<any> | yes |
| `rates` | object | yes |
| `resources` | object | yes |
| `schema` | string | yes |
| `spare_pools` | object | yes |
| `structure` | array<any> | yes |
| `summary` | object | yes |
| `system` | array<any> | yes |
| `total_changes` | integer | yes |
| `triggers` | object | yes |
| `truncated` | boolean | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_a": "<model_id_a>",
  "model_b": "<model_id_b>",
  "detail": "summary"
}
```

Build a standalone model from one hierarchy (a port extension), or just

The hierarchy's In node becomes Start and its Out node End, so its input is
always available. Hazards at the boundary -- elements following something

| `count` | integer | no |
| `hazards` | array<any> | no |
| `isolation` | object | no |
| `model_id` | string | no |

<a id="tool-get_element"></a>

#### `get_element`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Read one block, node, event, hierarchy or link back in full.

`selector` is an element name or 'Block:N' / 'Node:N' / 'Event:N' /
'Hier:N' / 'Link:N' (links have no name; use their id).  This is the
read counterpart of `update_element`: every field uses the friendly name
`update_element` accepts.

A block returns its connections (upstream/downstream), `failure` and
`repair` (distribution name, named parameters, mean/stdev), any
`logistics_delay` before/after repair, `sparing`, `maintenance`,
`dependency` and `phasing`.  `dependency` says what the block follows
(a block, node, event, hierarchy, its own node, or the whole system),
the % split of what happens when that goes down (nothing / idle / pm /
failure) and a plain-English `meaning`.  detail='full' adds costs,
growth/decay and standby stress.

A distribution's mean/stdev is null (with a note) when it has no finite
value for those parameters, e.g. a Pearson 5 with shape <= 2.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `detail` | string | no | `summary` | `summary`, `full` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `selector` | string | yes | — | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dependency` | object | no |
| `div_flow` | integer | no |
| `downstream` | array<any> | no |
| `failure` | object | no |
| `full_flow` | integer | no |
| `id` | integer | yes |
| `k` | integer | no |
| `kind` | string | yes |
| `logistics_delay` | object | no |
| `maintenance` | object | no |
| `n` | integer | no |
| `name` | string | no |
| `node_type` | string | no |
| `parent` | integer | no |
| `phasing` | boolean | no |
| `position` | object | no |
| `repair` | object | no |
| `sparing` | object | no |
| `upstream` | array<any> | no |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "selector": "Pump",
  "detail": "full"
}
```

<a id="tool-manage_spare_pools"></a>

#### `manage_spare_pools`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Create, list, edit or delete a spare pool.

action='list' returns every pool. `action='add'` needs `name`;
`action='update'` patches only the fields you pass; `action='delete'`
refuses while a block still has Pooled sparing that names the pool.

These are the pools `configure_sparing(mode="pool")` draws from, with
the stock and lead-time quantities spares planning needs. Field names

<a id="tool-undo_last_edit"></a>

#### `undo_last_edit`

- **Kind:** destructive
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Step one edit back (multi-step: call again to go further back).

Every edit tool backs up the prior state first (up to 20 deep), so
repeated calls walk further back rather than repeating the same
restore. Each undo can itself be undone with `redo_last_edit`, until
a new edit is made -- which clears the redo history, same as any
other editor.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `restored_version` | integer | yes |
| `summary` | string | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>"
}
```

<a id="tool-update_element"></a>

#### `update_element`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Update fields on an element.

`selector` is an element name, 'Block:N' / 'Node:N' / 'Event:N', a link
('Link:N', which carries capacity: `nom_flow`, `max_flow`, `cap_pri`),
or an auxiliary row by name ('Pool:RackSpares', 'Resource:Crew',
'Trigger:Storm', 'Phase:Summer' -- the bare name works too).
`patch` accepts any friendly .rbds field (e.g. `fail_params`,
`pm_freq`, pool `stock`) or a raw column name, including indexed forms
like `repair_params[0]`.  `fail_dist`/`repair_dist` take a distribution
name ("Weibull") or a code.  To make a block dependent on another element
use `dep_type` (RBDBlock/RBDNode/RBDEvent/RBDHier), `dep_num` (the
target's id; -1 = own node, -2 = whole system) and the effect split
`dep_nothing`/`dep_idle`/`dep_pm`/`dep_fail` (percent); read it back
with `get_element`.

Numeric fields may be numbers OR expression strings such as
"50.0 + @Rate * 1.4  # basis"; expressions are resolved to a float and
their derivation is kept in the model's `formulas`.  Returns
{changed, warnings, element} where `element` is a compact
{id, name, kind} summary; pass full=true for every field of the element.

A value RAPTOR Studio's dialogs refuse (a PM stagger at or above the PM
frequency, a cost below 0, a name with a space, ...) is refused with
RAPTOR Studio's own message and the model is left unchanged. A problem the
model already had (a file written elsewhere) does not block other edits.

| `selector` | string | yes | — | — |

<a id="tool-update_elements"></a>

#### `update_elements`

- **Kind:** writes
- **Group:** [Build and edit](#tools-build-edit)

Update many elements with one save.

Same `selector` and `patch` semantics as `update_element`, but the whole
list is applied inside one workspace batch: the model is written once at
the end instead of once per element. On a large model this is the
difference between seconds and tens of minutes (one `update_element` on
a ~10k-element model costs ~10 s).

The batch is atomic: if any item is refused, the model is restored to
its state before the call and nothing is written.

Returns {updated, results: [{selector, id, name, kind, changed}]}.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `updates` | array<object> | yes | — | — |

Parameter notes:

- `updates` — List of {"selector": str, "patch": {...}} objects

**Returns**

`{updated, results: [{selector, id, name, kind, changed}]}`.

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "updates": [
    {
      "selector": "Pump",
      "patch": {
        "name": "Pump A"
      }
    },
    {
      "selector": "Valve",
      "patch": {
        "fail_params": [
          6000
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="tools-analysis"></a>

### Analysis

Check a model, solve its static subset exactly, test failures, and measure which parts matter.

<a id="tool-analytical_analysis"></a>

#### `analytical_analysis`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Analysis](#tools-analysis)

Solve the static subset of a model exactly.

**Reliability mode** is non-repairable: `R(t)`, density, hazard, MTTF,
BX life, conditional reliability and exact importance. **Availability
mode** is steady state for independent components with perfect repair:
`A_i = MTTF_i / (MTTF_i + MTTR_i)` and exact availability importance.

The solver supports series, parallel, mixed, k-of-n, bridge networks and
hierarchies. `hierarchy` analyses one hierarchy on its own: its In
node is treated as Start and its Out node as End, so its input is
assumed always available. It refuses
PM, spares, resources and non-Bernoulli events, and refuses standby,
phases or dependencies until you say how to treat them; use `simulate`
for the behaviours it still cannot represent. `standby="active"` keeps
cold-standby paths in service and `standby="absent"` removes them;
`phase` analyses a phased model as if it stayed in that phase.
`dependencies="up"` analyses each dependent element's own law as if the
dependency never blocked it, and `dependencies="down"` removes dependent
elements from the success path. Without `dependencies`, a model with
dependencies is refused. `at` defaults to the model's time-terminated
run length. `tau` adds the conditional reliability of a further mission
of that length after `at`.
`ignore_repairs` (same as `ignore=["repairs"]`) gives the first-failure
reliability of a repairable model.

The default solver limits are 5,000 blocks/events and 2,000,000 BDD
nodes (about 0.7 GB). `max_variables` and `max_bdd_nodes` override them;
`max_bdd_nodes` may go up to half of the machine's free memory at about
350 bytes a node, and a higher value is refused. Before building, a
progress message gives a size outlook: whether any junction's inputs
share blocks (the only way the diagram grows large) and which. Raising a
limit does not guarantee a solution, and the solver refuses rather than
approximate; solving one hierarchy at a time is usually better.

A long solve sends MCP progress notifications about once a second: one
percentage for the whole solve (building the diagram, then the
results), with the stage and the time left in the message.
`export_analytical` writes the same result to a spreadsheet.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `at` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `bx` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `dependencies` | string \| null | no | `null` | `up`, `down` |
| `equation` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `hierarchy` | string \| integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `ignore` | array<string> \| null | no | `null` | `repairs`, `pm`, `spares`, `resources` |
| `ignore_repairs` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `importance` | boolean | no | `true` | — |
| `max_bdd_nodes` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `max_variables` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `mode` | string | no | `reliability` | `reliability`, `availability` |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `phase` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `standby` | string \| null | no | `null` | `active`, `absent` |
| `tau` | number \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `times` | array<number> \| null | no | `null` | — |

Parameter notes:

- `at` — Defaults to the model's time-terminated run length.

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `applicable` | boolean | yes |
| `assumptions` | array<any> | yes |
| `availability` | number \| null | no |
| `bdd_nodes` | integer | yes |
| `bx` | object | no |
| `components` | array<any> | yes |
| `equation` | string \| null | no |
| `hazard` | number \| null | no |
| `hierarchy` | string \| null | no |
| `importance` | array<any> | yes |
| `mode` | string | yes |
| `model` | string | yes |
| `mttf` | number \| null | no |
| `pdf` | number \| null | no |
| `reliability` | number \| null | no |
| `schema` | string | yes |
| `scope` | object | yes |
| `time` | number \| null | yes |
| `unavailability` | number \| null | no |
| `units` | string | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "mode": "reliability",
  "at": 500,
  "importance": true
}
```

<a id="tool-describe_metrics"></a>

#### `describe_metrics`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Analysis](#tools-analysis)

List the result metrics, and optionally show one run's values.

Without `run_id`, returns the name and units of every metric RAPTOR
reports: availability, reliability, conditional reliability,
dependability, MTBDE/MDT, MTBM/MTBMs/MTBMu, MMT/MMTs/MMTu, system and
component failures, and green/yellow/red percentages, plus, for a run
with capacity analysis, units produced, mean flow and capacity,
capacity-weighted availability (mean flow / flow generated) and lost
flow, plus, for a run with cost analysis, grand total, system down cost
and system lost-flow cost. **Definitions and
equations are not repeated here** -- call `read_doc('formulas')` for
them; that page is the single source. With `run_id`, also returns that
run's sample count, min/mean/max, standard deviation and standard
error. `model_id` is optional and only checks that the run belongs to
that model.

These are the engine's existing outputs; no analytical or alternative
solution method is applied. Use `get_report` or `get_table` for the
underlying data. Censored MTBDE/MTBM values are lower bounds and are
marked with `>` in the Markdown view.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `run_id` | string \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `isolation` | object | no |
| `metrics` | array<any> | yes |
| `model_hash` | string | no |
| `model_id` | string | no |
| `notes` | array<any> | no |
| `run_id` | string | no |
| `runs` | integer | no |
| `units` | string | no |

**Example**

```json
{
  "run_id": "<run_id>"
}
```

<a id="tool-failure_effects"></a>

#### `failure_effects`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Analysis](#tools-analysis)

Run failure-effects analysis (Raptor workbook Chapter 10).

Fails and/or repairs the listed blocks or events and reports the resulting
system status and the Failure Effects text (failed, induced, idle and PM
components, down and degraded nodes). A phased model starts in phase 1;
`phase` moves it to another phase first. Returns {system_status, affected,
log, effects, criticality, phase}, plus, for a model with capacity
analysis, `capacity`: {flow_generated, delivered, lost,
delivered_fraction, system_capacity, nodes: [{id, name, flow,
capacity}]} -- the flow the state delivers, as capacity analysis would
record it.

Each call is an **independent scenario starting from the all-good
state**: it does not accumulate failures across calls.  To test
several simultaneous failures, name them all in one `fail` list; a
`repair` can only undo a failure named in the same call.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fail` | array<string \| integer> \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `phase` | integer \| null | no | `null` | — |
| `repair` | array<string \| integer> \| null | no | `null` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `affected` | array<any> | yes |
| `capacity` | object | no |
| `criticality` | number | yes |
| `effects` | object | yes |
| `log` | array<any> | yes |
| `phase` | integer \| null | yes |
| `system_status` | string | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "fail": [
    "Pump"
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-failure_effects_batch"></a>

#### `failure_effects_batch`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Analysis](#tools-analysis)

Run many failure-effects scenarios in one call, on one model set-up.

`scenarios` is a list of `{"fail": [...], "repair": [...], "phase": N}`
(every key optional), up to 2000. Each scenario is independent and starts
from the all-good state, exactly as a separate `failure_effects` call
would; the model is only set up once, so hundreds of combinations on a
large model take seconds, not one set-up each.

Returns {model_id, count, failed, scenarios}. `scenarios[i]` has the
scenario's `index`, `fail` and `repair`, then either its result
({system_status, affected, effects, criticality, phase}, `capacity` for
a model with capacity analysis, plus the `log` text when `include_log`
is true) or `{"error": ...}` when that scenario
could not be applied (an unknown or already-failed element, a bad
phase). A bad scenario does not stop the others. `failed` counts them.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `include_log` | boolean | no | `false` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `scenarios` | array<object> | yes | — | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | integer | yes |
| `failed` | integer | yes |
| `model_id` | string | yes |
| `scenarios` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>",
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "fail": [
        "Pump"
      ]
    },
    {
      "fail": [
        "Pump",
        "Valve"
      ]
    },
    {
      "fail": [
        "Pump"
      ],
      "repair": [
        "Valve"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="tool-single_point_failures"></a>

#### `single_point_failures`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Analysis](#tools-analysis)

Find single-point failures in the model.

A single point failure is an element whose failure alone takes the
system down, found as Raptor does (by failing each element in Failure
Effects View, so dependencies and cold standby count). Returns
{spofs, count, total, offset, next_offset, elapsed_seconds, cached};
each spof is {kind, id, name, crit} plus `phase` for a phased model.

`limit` pages the response (default 100, use 0 for all); the full row
set is still computed and cached by model content, so later pages and
repeated calls are instant. `workers > 1` parallelises the candidate
tests on an unphased model.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | integer | no | `100` | — |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |
| `offset` | integer | no | `0` | — |
| `workers` | integer | no | `1` | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cached` | boolean | yes |
| `count` | integer | yes |
| `elapsed_seconds` | number | yes |
| `next_offset` | integer \| null | yes |
| `offset` | integer | yes |
| `spofs` | array<any> | yes |
| `total` | integer | yes |

**Example**

```json
{
  "model_id": "<model_id>"
}
```

<a id="tool-validate_model"></a>

#### `validate_model`

- **Kind:** read-only
- **Group:** [Analysis](#tools-analysis)

Validate a model for structural and parameter errors.

Returns {errors, warnings, groups, runnable}. `groups` collapses the
same rule firing on many elements into one row (rule, count, example
elements), which is what makes a 700-error model readable; `errors`
and `warnings` keep the verbatim per-element list. Always call this
before a run.

**Parameters**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Schema default | Enum / allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model_id` | string | yes | — | — |

**Returns**

| Field | Type | Always present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `errors` | array<any> | yes |
| `groups` | array<any> | yes |
| `runnable` | boolean | yes |
| `warnings` | array<any> | yes |

**Example**

```json

  "model_id": "<model_id>"
```
